units.title: Functions and Types
units.tip: Haskell is built around pure functions: functions that always return the same output for the same input and never change the state of the program. Every function has a type, and a type signature spells out what types it accepts and returns.

exercises.question: What is a pure function?
exercises.answer: A function that always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects
exercises.explain: A pure function depends only on its inputs and never modifies global state or produces side effects. This makes code predictable and testable.
choices: A function that always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects
A function declared with the keyword pure
A function that returns a pure value

exercises.question: Which of these is a side effect?
exercises.answer: Printing to the screen or modifying a global variable
exercises.explain: Side effects are actions that change the state of the program or interact with the outside world. Pure functions avoid them.
choices: Printing to the screen or modifying a global variable

exercises.question: Is this function pure? double x = x * 2
exercises.answer: Yes, it always returns 2x for any input x
exercises.explain: This function takes x and returns 2x every time. It has no side effects and depends only on its input.
choices: No, because it is too simple
No, because x is a variable
Yes, it always returns 2x for any input x

exercises.question: Why are pure functions useful in Haskell?
exercises.answer: They are predictable, testable, and easier to reason about
exercises.explain: Pure functions eliminate hidden dependencies and side effects, making code easier to understand, test, and parallelize.
choices: They do not need to be debugged
They run faster than impure functions
They are predictable, testable, and easier to reason about

exercises.question: What does immutability mean in Haskell?
exercises.answer: Once a variable is bound to a value, it cannot be changed
exercises.explain: In Haskell, variables are immutable. If you want a different value, you create a new variable. This eliminates a whole class of bugs.
choices: Once a variable is bound to a value, it cannot be changed
Variables must be declared before use
Variables must have a type annotation

exercises.question: What is a type signature?
exercises.answer: A declaration stating what types a function accepts and returns
exercises.explain: A type signature like add :: Int -> Int -> Int tells you the function accepts two Ints and returns an Int. The :: means has type.
choices: A comment explaining what the function does
A declaration stating what types a function accepts and returns

exercises.question: What does the -> in a type signature mean?
exercises.answer: Separates argument types from the return type
exercises.explain: In add :: Int -> Int -> Int, the arrows separate parameters and lead to the return type. Int -> Int -> Int means two Ints, returns Int.
choices: Assigns a value to a variable
Separates argument types from the return type

exercises.question: What does this type signature mean? greet :: String -> String
exercises.answer: A function that takes a String and returns a String
exercises.explain: greet accepts one String argument and returns a String. For example, greet might add Hello to the input.
choices: A function that returns two Strings
A function that takes a String and returns a String

exercises.question: Why are type signatures important in Haskell?
exercises.answer: They make code explicit, enable compiler checking, and serve as documentation
exercises.explain: Type signatures tell the compiler what types are expected, catch errors before runtime, and tell the next programmer what a function does.
choices: They make code explicit, enable compiler checking, and serve as documentation
They reduce the amount of code

exercises.question: What is the return type of this function? add x y = x + y
exercises.answer: Numeric types like Int or Double, depending on the input
exercises.explain: If x and y are Ints, the result is Int. If they are Doubles, the result is Double. This is called polymorphism.
choices: Numeric types like Int or Double, depending on the input

units.title: Lists and Pattern Matching
units.tip: Lists are the backbone of Haskell. A list is either empty or a head element followed by a tail (another list). Pattern matching lets you destructure lists and other data, extracting the values you need.

exercises.question: What is a list in Haskell?
exercises.answer: An ordered collection of elements of the same type
exercises.explain: [1, 2, 3] is a list of numbers. ["apple", "banana"] is a list of Strings. All elements must have the same type.
choices: An ordered collection of elements of the same type

exercises.question: What is the empty list?
exercises.answer: [] (square brackets with nothing inside)
exercises.explain: [] is the empty list. Every finite list is built by adding elements onto [], so [1, 2] is really 1 : (2 : []).

exercises.question: What does the : operator do in Haskell?
exercises.answer: Prepends an element to the front of a list (cons operator)
exercises.explain: 1 : [2, 3] gives [1, 2, 3]. It puts the element on the left at the head and the list on the right as the tail.
choices: Prepends an element to the front of a list (cons operator)
Appends an element to the end

exercises.question: How do you concatenate two lists?
exercises.answer: Using the ++ operator: [1, 2] ++ [3, 4] gives [1, 2, 3, 4]
exercises.explain: The ++ operator joins two lists. The first list is traversed to find its end, then the second list is attached.

exercises.question: What type does the list [True, False, True] have?
exercises.answer: [Bool] (a list of Bools)
exercises.explain: [Bool] means a list of Bools. In the same way, ["a", "b"] has type [String], a list of Strings.

exercises.question: What is pattern matching?
exercises.answer: Destructuring data by matching it against a pattern
exercises.explain: Pattern matching lets you extract values from structures. For example, matching [1, 2, 3] against (x:xs) binds x to 1 and xs to [2, 3].
choices: Finding text patterns in a string
Checking if two values are equal
Destructuring data by matching it against a pattern

exercises.question: What does (x:xs) match against in pattern matching?
exercises.answer: A non-empty list, binding the head to x and the tail to xs
exercises.explain: For [1, 2, 3], the pattern (x:xs) binds x = 1 and xs = [2, 3]. It matches any list that has at least one element.
choices: A non-empty list, binding the head to x and the tail to xs

exercises.question: What is a list comprehension?
exercises.answer: A concise syntax for creating lists by applying an expression to elements
exercises.explain: [x * 2 | x <- [1, 2, 3]] creates [2, 4, 6] by doubling each element. The <- means drawn from.
choices: A concise syntax for creating lists by applying an expression to elements
A way to comment on lists

exercises.question: What does this list comprehension produce? [x | x <- [1..5], x > 2]
exercises.explain: x <- [1..5] iterates over 1 to 5, and x > 2 filters to keep only values greater than 2.

exercises.question: What list does the range [1..10] produce?
exercises.explain: The range [1..10] generates the numbers from 1 to 10, including both ends. A step can be given too: [1, 3..9] gives [1, 3, 5, 7, 9].

units.title: Recursion
units.tip: Recursion is how Haskell handles repetition. A recursive function calls itself with simpler inputs until it reaches a base case that stops the recursion. Every recursive function needs a base case and a recursive case.

exercises.question: What is recursion?
exercises.answer: A function calling itself with simpler inputs until reaching a base case
exercises.explain: Recursion breaks a problem into smaller versions of itself. factorial n = n * factorial (n - 1) keeps shrinking n until it reaches a base case such as factorial 0 = 1.
choices: A function calling itself with simpler inputs until reaching a base case

exercises.question: What is a base case in recursion?
exercises.answer: The stopping condition that prevents infinite recursion
exercises.explain: Without a base case, a recursive function would call itself forever. For factorial, the base case is factorial 0 = 1.
choices: The stopping condition that prevents infinite recursion
The first line of the function

exercises.question: What is the base case for this recursive function? mySum [] = 0; mySum (x:xs) = x + mySum xs
exercises.answer: mySum [] = 0, which stops recursion when the list is empty
exercises.explain: When the list is empty, we return 0 instead of calling mySum again. This stops the recursion.
choices: mySum [] = 0, which stops recursion when the list is empty

exercises.question: How many times is mySum called for mySum [1, 2, 3]?
exercises.answer: 4 times: mySum [1,2,3], mySum [2,3], mySum [3], and mySum []
exercises.explain: Each call peels off the first element. When the list becomes empty, the base case mySum [] = 0 stops it.
choices: 4 times: mySum [1,2,3], mySum [2,3], mySum [3], and mySum []

exercises.question: What does this recursive function do? len [] = 0; len (_:xs) = 1 + len xs
exercises.answer: Counts the number of elements in a list
exercises.explain: The underscore _ ignores the head. We add 1 for each element and recurse on the tail until the list is empty.
choices: Counts the number of elements in a list

exercises.question: What is tail recursion?
exercises.answer: Recursion where the recursive call is the last operation
exercises.explain: In tail recursion, the result of the recursive call is returned immediately. The compiler can optimize it to not use extra stack space.
choices: Recursion at the end of a file
Recursion where the recursive call is the last operation

exercises.question: Is this tail recursive? mySum [] = 0; mySum (x:xs) = x + mySum xs
exercises.answer: No, because the recursive call is not the last operation (+ is applied after)
exercises.explain: The result of mySum xs is used in x + mySum xs, so this is not tail recursive. A tail recursive version would accumulate the total as a parameter.
choices: No, because the recursive call is not the last operation (+ is applied after)
Only if the list is short

exercises.question: What is an accumulator in tail recursion?
exercises.answer: An extra parameter that builds up the result as we recurse
exercises.explain: An accumulator collects intermediate results. sumAcc [] acc = acc; sumAcc (x:xs) acc = sumAcc xs (x + acc) uses acc as an accumulator.
choices: A list of all previous results
A keyword that marks a function as tail recursive
An extra parameter that builds up the result as we recurse

exercises.question: Why can tail recursion be more efficient than regular recursion?
exercises.answer: The compiler can optimize it to reuse the same stack frame, avoiding stack overflow
exercises.explain: Tail recursion can be compiled to a loop. Regular recursion stacks up frames, potentially causing stack overflow on deep recursion. In Haskell the accumulator often needs to be evaluated strictly to get this benefit.
choices: The compiler can optimize it to reuse the same stack frame, avoiding stack overflow
It uses less memory for the data

exercises.question: What is the advantage of recursion over loops in functional programming?
exercises.answer: It works naturally with immutable data, since each call binds new values instead of changing old ones
exercises.explain: A loop usually updates a counter in place, which is mutation. Recursion passes new values into each call, so nothing is changed, which fits immutable data.
choices: It works naturally with immutable data, since each call binds new values instead of changing old ones
Recursion never needs a base case

units.title: Higher-Order Functions
units.tip: Higher-order functions accept functions as arguments or return functions as results. map applies a function to each list element, filter selects elements, and fold reduces a list to a single value. These are the workhorse functions of functional programming.

exercises.question: What is a higher-order function?
exercises.answer: A function that takes a function as an argument or returns a function
exercises.explain: map, filter, and fold are higher-order because they accept a function (like (+ 1) or (> 5)) as an argument.
choices: A function that is called many times
A function with a high return value
A function that takes a function as an argument or returns a function

exercises.question: What does map do?
exercises.answer: Applies a function to each element of a list and returns a new list
exercises.explain: map (*2) [1, 2, 3] applies (*2) to each element, giving [2, 4, 6].
choices: Finds an element in a list
Applies a function to each element of a list and returns a new list

exercises.question: What does filter do?
exercises.answer: Selects elements from a list that satisfy a condition
exercises.explain: filter (> 5) [1, 3, 7, 2, 9] keeps only elements > 5, returning [7, 9].
choices: Selects elements from a list that satisfy a condition

exercises.question: What is the result of map (+ 1) [1, 2, 3]?
exercises.explain: map applies (+ 1) to each element, so 1 becomes 2, 2 becomes 3, and 3 becomes 4.

exercises.question: What is the result of filter even [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]? (even is a built-in function that checks whether a number is even)
exercises.explain: filter even keeps only elements where even returns True, so only 2 and 4 are kept.

exercises.question: What does a fold, such as foldl, do?
exercises.answer: Reduces a list to a single value by applying a function cumulatively
exercises.explain: foldl (+) 0 [1, 2, 3] starts with 0, adds 1 to get 1, adds 2 to get 3, adds 3 to get 6.
choices: Reduces a list to a single value by applying a function cumulatively

exercises.question: What is the result of foldl (+) 0 [1, 2, 3, 4]?
What does function composition do?
exercises.answer: Combines two functions into one by applying them in sequence
exercises.explain: f . g means apply g first, then f to the result. If f x = x * 2 and g x = x + 1, then (f . g) 5 = f (g 5) = f 6 = 12.
choices: Combines two functions into one by applying them in sequence

exercises.question: What is the . operator called?
exercises.answer: The composition operator
exercises.explain: The . operator composes functions. f . g reads as f after g.

exercises.question: What does map ((*2) . (+1)) [1, 2, 3] return?
exercises.explain: For each element, first add 1, then multiply by 2. 1 becomes 2, then 4. 2 becomes 3, then 6. 3 becomes 4, then 8.

units.title: The Type System
units.tip: Haskell's type system goes beyond just Int and String. Maybe represents an optional value (a Maybe Int is either Nothing or Just with an Int inside, like Just 5). Type classes group types that share behavior, like Eq for equality or Ord for ordering.

exercises.question: What is the Maybe type?
exercises.answer: A type that represents an optional value: either Just a value or Nothing
exercises.explain: A Maybe Int is either Just 5 (has a value) or Nothing (no value). It is safer than null in other languages because the type shows when a value might be missing.
choices: A type that represents an optional value: either Just a value or Nothing
A type that is always Nothing

exercises.question: What does Just 5 mean?
exercises.answer: A Maybe value that contains the number 5
exercises.explain: Just wraps a value inside a Maybe. Just 5 is a Maybe holding the number 5.
choices: A Maybe value that contains the number 5
A tuple of the word Just and the number 5

exercises.question: What does Nothing mean?
exercises.answer: A Maybe value that represents the absence of a value
exercises.explain: Nothing is used when there is no value to return. For example, searching a list for an element that is not there gives Nothing.
choices: A Maybe value that represents the absence of a value

exercises.question: Why does Haskell use Maybe where many other languages use null?
exercises.answer: Because it makes optional values explicit and makes the programmer deal with the Nothing case
exercises.explain: Maybe makes missing values explicit in the type. You cannot use a Maybe Int as a plain Int, so you have to deal with the Nothing case, usually by pattern matching.
choices: Because zero cannot be stored in an ordinary type
Because Maybe and null mean exactly the same thing
Because it lets the program ignore missing values
Because it makes optional values explicit and makes the programmer deal with the Nothing case

exercises.question: What is the type of Just True?
exercises.answer: Maybe Bool
exercises.explain: Just True has type Maybe Bool. The Just constructor wraps a Bool inside a Maybe.

exercises.question: What is a type class?
exercises.answer: A group of types that share common behavior or operations
exercises.explain: Eq is a type class for equality. All types in Eq support ==. Ord is a type class for ordering, supporting <, >, etc.
choices: A class used in object-oriented programming
A group of types that share common behavior or operations
A module that groups related functions

exercises.question: What does the Eq type class provide?
exercises.answer: The == and /= operators for comparing equality
exercises.explain: Any type in Eq supports == (equality) and /= (inequality). Int, String, and many others are instances of Eq.
choices: The == and /= operators for comparing equality

exercises.question: What does the Ord type class provide?
exercises.answer: Ordering operators like <, >, <=, >= and the compare function
exercises.explain: Ord lets you compare values. compare 5 3 returns GT (greater than), compare 2 2 returns EQ (equal).
choices: Ordering operators like <, >, <=, >= and the compare function

exercises.question: What does this type signature mean? sort :: Ord a => [a] -> [a]
exercises.answer: sort works on any list where the element type is in the Ord class
exercises.explain: Ord a => means the type a must be an instance of Ord. So sort [3, 1, 2] works, and so does sorting a list of Strings, but a list of functions cannot be sorted because functions have no ordering.
choices: sort works on any list where the element type is in the Ord class
sort works only on lists of numbers
sort turns a list into a single Ord value
sort works on lists of any type

exercises.question: What does it mean for a function to be polymorphic?
exercises.answer: It works on values of many different types instead of just one
exercises.explain: map works on a list of any element type, and sort works on any list whose elements can be ordered (Ord). One definition covers many types.
choices: It works on values of many different types instead of just one
It changes its own type while the program runs
It must be rewritten separately for every type

units.title: Lazy Evaluation
units.tip: Haskell evaluates expressions only when needed, not all at once. This is called lazy evaluation. It allows you to work with infinite lists and avoid unnecessary computation. You do not pay to compute values you never use.

exercises.question: What is lazy evaluation?
exercises.answer: Evaluating expressions only when their values are needed
exercises.explain: In Haskell, if you define x = 1 + 2 but never use x, the addition is never computed. This is different from eager languages that compute immediately.
choices: Evaluating expressions only when their values are needed
Skipping type checks until the program runs

exercises.question: What is the main benefit of lazy evaluation?
exercises.answer: You can work with infinite data structures and avoid unnecessary computation
exercises.explain: You can define [1..] (an infinite list) because elements are generated only as you access them. Unused computations are skipped entirely.
choices: No benefit, it is just different
You can work with infinite data structures and avoid unnecessary computation

exercises.question: Which definition creates an infinite list of 1s?
exercises.answer: ones = 1 : ones
exercises.explain: ones = 1 : ones creates [1, 1, 1, ...] infinitely, because the list is its own tail. Each element is generated when accessed, so take 5 ones gives [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. The built-in repeat 1 does the same job.

exercises.question: What does take 3 [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] return?
exercises.explain: take n lst returns the first n elements of a list. take 3 [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] returns [1, 2, 3].

exercises.question: Can you safely write take 5 [1..]?
exercises.answer: Yes, take 5 [1..] returns [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] without infinite loops
exercises.explain: take 5 terminates after 5 elements, so [1..] (infinite) is safe to use with take. Lazy evaluation ensures the list is generated only as needed.
choices: Yes, take 5 [1..] returns [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] without infinite loops
Only if you sort the list first

exercises.question: What is a thunk?
exercises.answer: An unevaluated computation deferred until its value is needed
exercises.explain: When Haskell sees an expression like 1 + 2, it creates a thunk (a suspended computation). When you actually need the value, it is evaluated.
choices: An unevaluated computation deferred until its value is needed

exercises.question: Why might lazy evaluation cause unexpected memory usage?
exercises.answer: Thunks accumulate, building up unevaluated computations that consume memory
exercises.explain: If you build a large structure of thunks without forcing evaluation, they pile up. This is called a space leak.
choices: Thunks accumulate, building up unevaluated computations that consume memory
It has no effect on memory

exercises.question: What happens when you evaluate head (map (*2) [1..])?
exercises.answer: It returns 2, because only the first element is ever computed
exercises.explain: map is lazy, so it produces its result one element at a time as each is asked for. head asks for just the first, so 1 * 2 is computed and the rest of [1..] is never touched.
choices: It never finishes, because map must double every element first
It returns 2, because only the first element is ever computed
It returns an error, because the list is infinite
It returns the whole list [2, 4, 6, ...] at once

exercises.question: What does filter (> 5) [1..] return?
exercises.answer: An infinite list of numbers greater than 5, computed only as they are accessed
exercises.explain: filter (> 5) [1..] returns an infinite list of numbers greater than 5. Each element is computed lazily when accessed.
choices: An infinite list of numbers greater than 5, computed only as they are accessed
It tries to filter the whole list first and hangs

exercises.question: Why is take important when working with infinite lists?
exercises.answer: It limits the result to a finite number of elements, so evaluation can stop
exercises.explain: take limits evaluation to a finite prefix of an infinite list, making infinite lists practical to use without hanging.
choices: It limits the result to a finite number of elements, so evaluation can stop
